title: Shield grassland you can see
items: Grassland that gives a bonus shield now shows a small shield badge in the corner of the tile, so you can tell it apart from plain grassland at a glance.

title: Rules closer to Civ 3
items: Tribal villages: barbarians come out most of the time, but Expansionist civilizations only find good things. Villages can now give Settlers or even turn into a city, both rarely.
Free advances: you get the advance you are researching, and Theory of Evolution's second advance is your free pick.
Golden ages: a great wonder that matches one of your traits has a 50% chance to start one.
Switching production costs nothing, extra shields after finishing something are lost, and rivers no longer link cities or resources (only roads do).
Corruption uses a city's real distance even without a road. A tile between two cities goes to the city with the strongest culture pull, weaker further away.
Capture: a size 1 city survives if its food box is at least half full, a captured Settler becomes two Workers, and barbarians never destroy a city.

Diplomacy: rivals may demand that your troops leave their land or pay tribute, refusing can mean war, breaking any treaty hurts your standing with everyone, and you can trade away your last copy of a resource.

title: Workers at work
items: Workers now visibly work on the map while they build roads, mines, irrigation and the rest: they swing their tools in a steady rhythm and each strike throws up earth, stones, wood chips or water, depending on the job. With "Reduce motion" switched on they stand still as before.

title: Click a tile to move there
items: With a unit selected, a left click on an empty tile sends the unit there, the same as Go to. Clicking your own units or cities still selects them, and right-click still moves or attacks as before.

title: Irrigation next to cities
items: Workers can now irrigate land next to a city that sits on a river or by a lake: the city counts as irrigated, so water spreads on from it. Diagonal neighbours count as water sources too. Automated workers and rival civilizations use this too.

title: Random civilization and remembered setup
items: The New game screen has a Random choice for your civilization: a civilization is picked for you when the game starts.

The New game screen remembers your choices: world, climate, civilization (including Random), difficulty, rivals, game type and victories start as you left them last time. The map seed stays fresh so every game gets a new world.

title: Ground textures fix
items: The ground no longer turns black a few seconds into a game: the painted terrain textures now load and show as intended.

title: Civilopedia, advisors and polish
items: The Civilopedia (F10, or the small ? next to a name): a page for every unit, building, wonder, advance, government, terrain, resource and civilization, and thirty articles on how the game works. Search with the / key; right-click anything in the build list or the science advisor to look it up.
Your advisors speak up: short tips the first time something comes up, from founding your capital to pollution. Switch them off or hear them all again in Settings.
Settings for everyone: interface size, a light theme, colours that colour-blind players can tell apart, and less motion.
The draft: once you know Nationalism, cities can turn a citizen into a conscript defender (the city screen has the button).

Closer to the original rules: SAM batteries guard against air strikes, walls protect people and buildings from bombardment, Philosophy gives its discoverer a free advance, Satellites reveal the map, disbanding in a city helps its build, and every civilization starts with its own scout where it has one.
Rival civilizations settle faster in the early game and draft defenders when threatened, and big maps play faster between turns.
Tribal villages no longer release barbarians while you have only one city.
Q and E now give the Reinforce front and Escort orders when a unit has them; otherwise they still turn the camera.

title: Art and sound
items: The land is painted: grassland, plains, desert, tundra, hills, mountains, forests, jungles, marshes and beaches now have hand-painted ground instead of flat colour.
Music for every era and the title screen, and the sounds of the land under the camera: meadows, forests, deserts, snow, the sea and busy towns.

Every event in the game has a sound now, from marching feet and hoofbeats to fallen soldiers, upgrades, timber, treaties and warnings. The Sound menu sets effects, music and ambience apart (Ctrl+M mutes).
Every unit has a portrait, including all unique units; kings show their ruler, and the barbarians have a chieftain.
Fortresses and barricades stand on the map, and the Indian war elephant and the Arab camel riders have their own models.

New unit orders: Reinforce front (Q) sends a unit to the city enemies press hardest, Escort (E) keeps a unit beside another, and Interception duty (Shift+I) keeps a fighter on watch every turn of a war.
The automation lens (Lens, Ctrl+K) shows what every automated unit and city is doing.
The calendar now ends in AD 2050 on the last turn, as it should, and big maps play faster between turns.

title: Civilizations, golden ages and every way to win
items: Every civilization plays differently: two traits each (militaristic, religious, commercial, industrious, expansionist, scientific, agricultural, seafaring), its own unique unit, two free advances and its own city names. The new-game screen shows them.
Golden ages: your unique unit's first victory, or wonders matching both your traits, bring 20 turns of extra shields and commerce.
Great scientists join scientific civilizations that are first to an advance, and every great leader has a name.
Conquered cities may resist, and cities can change sides when a neighbour's culture outshines yours. Watch the badges on the city screen.
Pollution, nuclear meltdowns and global warming arrive with industry.
The space race, the United Nations, domination, culture and the histograph: the new victory screen (F8) shows how close everyone is, with the score history and the spaceship.
New game modes: regicide, mass regicide, elimination and victory points, and each victory can be switched off.
The remaining wonder effects work: the Great Library, Wall Street, the Great Lighthouse, Magellan's Voyage and wonders that draw visitors.
Rivals use their unique units, build wonders for their golden age, race to space, and keep their armies affordable so their cities grow.

title: Automation: hand the empire to your advisors
items: The new automation screen (F7) hands whole parts of the game to automation: citizens, builds, workers, research, the treasury, the military and answers to offers. One click delegates everything; changing something by hand pauses automation just there.

City governors place citizens for a goal: Balanced, Growth, Production, Gold, Science, Culture, Military Pump, Settler Pump or your own weights. They keep cities fed and out of disorder and may rush builds within a budget.

Build templates (New town, Core city, Coastal, Frontier fortress and more) choose what cities build, with conditions such as "Temple if unhappy" or "best defender if at war". Copy one to make your own; new and captured cities get one automatically.

Workers share one pool: they connect resources and cities, irrigate hungry cities, mine weak producers, clean pollution and keep away from enemies. The job board shows who works where and why, and regions keep them off jobs you forbid.
New unit orders: garrison the nearest city that needs defenders, patrol between two tiles, bombard enemies in range every turn, and rally points for each city.
Your own rules: "when a city grows to 12 without a hospital, build one", "new scouts explore". Rules and templates export to a file you can share.
Each turn opens with a digest: what needs you, most urgent first, and what automation took care of. A 200-city empire now takes seconds a turn.
Set a research goal in the science advisor and automation takes the steps toward it. Every automated order explains itself in the log.
Traded luxuries and strategic resources now need a trade route between the two capitals; stealth bombers choose which unit to strike.

title: Rivals: computer leaders, diplomacy and espionage
items: Play as one of 31 civilizations; every rival is led by a computer player with its own leader's temper, favourite government and build preferences.
The computer players expand, defend their cities, research, trade advances among themselves, form alliances, and raise armies that besiege and storm enemy cities.
Meet other civilizations as your explorers and borders reach theirs. The new diplomacy screen (F4) shows each leader's mood, from furious to gracious, and the reasons behind it.
Trade advances, gold, gold per turn, world maps, contacts, embassies, luxuries and strategic resources, even cities. Ask a leader "What would you want?" to hear their price.
Treaties: peace, ceasefires, right of passage, mutual protection pacts, alliances against a common enemy, and embargoes. Peace now needs the other side's agreement.
Reputation: breaking a fresh peace treaty or a pact is remembered by every civilization; defaulting on payments costs trust.
Espionage: open embassies, investigate cities, steal advances and world maps, plant spies, sabotage production and turn cities with propaganda.
Difficulty levels now give computer players Civ3's handicaps: extra start units, extra unit support and cheaper research at the higher levels.
Paratroopers jump from cities, units are airlifted between airports, submarines and stealth aircraft pick their targets, and barbarians land from the sea.
The war room moved to F3; advances already known to civilizations you have met cost less to research.

title: First alpha: war comes to the world
items: Combat by the Civ3 rules: round-by-round battles with hit points by experience, terrain, river, fortress, fortification and city defences, and retreat for fast units.
See your odds before you attack, with every modifier on both sides.
Capture or raze cities, plunder gold, take workers and artillery as prizes; civilizations can be destroyed.
Catapults to battleships bombard; bombers, fighters and reconnaissance fly missions; anti-air fire and interceptors defend.
Ships carry troops, armies are formed by great leaders born in battle, and leaders can hurry a wonder.
Barbarian camps appear in the wilds and raid nearby cities; tribal villages may now teach an advance or hide barbarians.
War weariness unsettles republics and democracies; the war room (F4) declares war and makes peace.
Nuclear weapons once the Manhattan Project stands somewhere, with missile defence.
New 3D models for every line of units from swordsmen to carriers, health bars and battle effects on the map.
Already in place: a 3D world map with rivers and fog of war, cities with growth, production, corruption, happiness, science, governments, culture and borders.
